name: Staged Pipeline
summary: Sequential stages, each reporting its own elapsed time, with a failure shown in place and everything after it marked skipped rather than left looking pending.

attempts.prompt: Build a multi-stage progress indicator for a deploy pipeline.
attempts.problem: A single bar filling from zero to a hundred, which throws away the only thing a staged process knows that a spinner does not: which stage it is in. Nothing reported how long any stage took, so a pipeline that always stalls on install looked identical to one that always stalls on tests.

attempts.prompt: Show each stage separately with its own state.
attempts.problem: Stages had states, but a failure replaced the whole component with an error panel, so the user lost the record of which stages had already succeeded — which is exactly the information needed to decide what to do next. Stages after the failure kept their pending appearance, implying they were still queued when they would never run.

finalPrompt:
Build a staged pipeline indicator in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies, with five sequential stages of differing durations, one of which fails.

Each stage shows its own state — waiting, running, done, failed, skipped — and its own elapsed time once it has run. Measure the time rather than printing the configured duration, since the measurement is the useful figure.

When a stage fails, do three things and no more. Mark that stage failed and state the reason inside it. Mark every later stage skipped with a distinct appearance, because a stage that will never run must not look like one that is about to. Leave every earlier stage showing its successful result, since which stages passed is exactly what the user needs to decide what happens next.

Never replace the component with an error panel. The record of what succeeded is the most valuable thing on screen at the moment something fails.

Offer retry from the failed stage, which resets that stage and everything after it and resumes from there, rather than restarting the whole pipeline.

Announce transitions through a role="status" region: the failure with its elapsed time and the fact that later stages were skipped, and completion when the run finishes. Do not announce every stage, which is noise on a five-stage pipeline.

The running indicator is a rotating partial ring built from a border with one transparent side. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, stop the rotation and show a static ring rather than swapping in different markup.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--bg), var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent), var(--mono). No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
Both failures come from treating an error as an event that replaces the screen rather than as a state of one item. The same mistake as the optimistic row, in a different shape, which is why it is worth naming as a rule: put the failure where the thing that failed is, and leave the surrounding context intact.

The skipped state is the detail that makes it feel finished. Without it the remaining stages sit in their pending style, quietly implying the run might continue, and the user waits for something that will never happen. It costs one loop and one CSS rule.

Measuring elapsed time rather than echoing the configured duration is a small honesty point with a practical payoff: the measured figure is the one that tells you which stage is actually slow.
